did_you_know.text: Did you know? This is the second banquet Esther holds for King Ahasuerus and Haman, at which she is about to reveal her request.
Did you know? The king again assures Esther that he will grant her question and request, even using the phrase “up to half the kingdom” to emphasize his willingness to give her what she asks.
Did you know? Esther distinguishes between her “question” and her “request”: in her question, she asks for her life, and in her request, she asks for her people to be saved.
Did you know? Esther explains that the danger is not merely slavery, but that she and her people have been sold for destruction, slaughter, and annihilation.

Did you know? Esther says that if she and her people had merely been sold as male and female slaves, she would have remained silent; in that case, she says, the matter would not have caused enough harm to justify troubling the king.
Did you know? After Esther reveals the danger, the king is not satisfied simply knowing that a decree exists; he explicitly asks who the man is who dared to do this.
Did you know? Esther points directly to Haman and calls him “a wicked and hostile man.” At her words, Haman is terrified before the king and queen.
Did you know? The king leaves angrily for the palace garden, while Haman realizes that disaster has been decreed against him and turns to Esther to plead for his life.
Did you know? When the king returns, he sees Haman falling on the couch where Esther is, and interprets the scene as an attempt to assault the queen even in the royal palace.
Did you know? Harbona reminds the king about the fifty-cubit-high gallows Haman had prepared for Mordecai, who had spoken favorably of the king.
Did you know? Haman is hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai, and at the end of the chapter, the king’s anger subsides.
